name: Paliperidone (Invega)
summary: A second-generation antipsychotic used for schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. Available as a daily extended-release tablet or long-acting injections that can last 1, 3, or 6 months.
description: Paliperidone helps reduce hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, disorganized thinking, and mood symptoms tied to psychosis. It’s available as a once-daily ER tablet (Invega) and as long-acting injections (Invega Sustenna monthly, Invega Trinza every 3 months, Invega Hafyera every 6 months; plus Erzofri as another monthly option). It can be very effective, but it comes with real risks—movement side effects (akathisia/parkinsonism), weight and metabolic changes, prolactin-related sexual/hormonal side effects, orthostatic dizziness/falls, and rare but dangerous reactions like neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It is NOT approved for dementia-related psychosis and carries an increased mortality warning in that population.
patient_summary: Paliperidone is an antipsychotic for schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. You can take it as a once-daily tablet or get it as a long-acting injection so you don’t have to remember pills every day. It can calm psychosis and stabilize functioning, but watch for restlessness, stiffness/shakiness, sleepiness, dizziness when standing, weight/metabolic changes, and prolactin side effects (sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, breast symptoms). It’s not approved for dementia-related psychosis and may increase mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.

linked_conditions.context: Used as monotherapy for schizophrenia. Oral ER is once daily; long-acting injections can improve adherence and reduce relapse risk tied to missed doses.
Can be used alone or alongside mood stabilizers or antidepressants when schizoaffective symptoms include mood episodes plus psychosis.
Sometimes used as an alternative option for acute mania or mixed features and for maintenance, based on clinical judgment and specialist input.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity (including anaphylaxis or angioedema) to paliperidone, risperidone, or any component of the formulation

efficacy_response.patient_text: Some people start noticing early changes within 1 to 2 weeks, but the bigger, more reliable improvements often build over 4 to 6 weeks—especially for thinking clarity, paranoia, and overall functioning.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral ER is absorbed slowly (extended-release). Long-acting injections release medication for weeks to months depending on the product.
pharmacokinetics.onset: Oral: early effects may show up within 1-2 weeks; continued improvement can build through 4-6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Oral: ~24 hours (extended-release). LAI peak timing varies by formulation.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Oral: ~23 hours (longer with reduced kidney function). LAI half-life is much longer and formulation-dependent.
pharmacokinetics.duration_XR: Oral ER: once daily. LAIs: monthly, 3-month, or 6-month coverage depending on product.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Limited hepatic metabolism; CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 play a minor role. Large portion eliminated unchanged.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: May be taken without regard to meals; follow product instructions for consistent use

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Paliperidone is an atypical antipsychotic used to treat psychotic disorders—mainly schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. It can help with hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, disorganized thinking, and mood symptoms that ride along with psychosis. It also exists in long-acting injectable forms, which can be a huge deal if daily pills are hard to stick with.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Ongoing psychosis symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, paranoia), disorganized thinking, and functional decline
{link:condition:schizoaffective-disorder:Schizoaffective disorder}: Psychosis plus mood episodes; can be used alone or with mood stabilizers/antidepressants
off_label: Acute mania or mixed episodes in bipolar disorder (alternative option; specialist-led)
Maintenance treatment in bipolar disorder (alternative option; specialist-led)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s nervous system has its own personality. Here’s what patients commonly describe with paliperidone (tablet or injection):

quotes: The voices didn’t vanish overnight, but they got less loud and less convincing.
Paranoia stopped running my day. I could reality-check again.
My brain felt less scrambled. I could follow conversations.
items.note: Early changes can show up within 1–2 weeks, but the more solid improvements often build over 4–6 weeks.

quotes: I felt calmer… but also kind of emotionally muted at first.
It took the edge off, but I had to dial in the dose so I didn’t feel like a zombie.
I wanted fewer symptoms, not fewer feelings—so we adjusted.
items.note: Finding the “enough to help, not so much it dulls you” dose is a real thing.

quotes: I couldn’t sit still. It felt like my legs had their own agenda.
I got stiff and slowed down, like my body was moving through molasses.
The shaking was subtle, but it was there—especially when we increased.
items.note: Akathisia, parkinsonism, dystonia, and dyskinesia can happen. The risk goes up with higher doses and sensitive patients.

quotes: I stood up and got that head-rush like I was about to black out.
The first couple weeks I had to go slow getting out of bed.
Hydration helped, but we also adjusted the titration pace.
items.note: Orthostatic hypotension can be worse with rapid titration and in older adults.

items.category: Hormones, sex drive, and prolactin side effects
quotes: My libido tanked and it felt out of nowhere.
My period got weird, and my doctor checked prolactin.
I hated that it helped my symptoms but messed with my body—so we talked options.
items.note: Paliperidone is known for a higher risk of prolactin elevation (sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, breast symptoms).

quotes: Not having to remember pills every day felt like freedom.
The injection site was sore for a day or two, but it was worth the stability.
It’s convenient—but dose changes take longer to show up, so patience matters.
items.note: With LAIs, adjustments can take months to fully show their effect because drug levels change slowly.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Paliperidone isn’t a “take it today, everything is fixed tonight” medication. It tends to work in layers—early calming first, then deeper improvements in thinking and psychosis symptoms over time.
key_points: 1–2 weeks: Early effects may be noticeable (sleep, agitation, intensity of paranoia/voices may start shifting)
4–6 weeks: More reliable, meaningful improvement often builds here
Oral ER tablet: Taken once daily; steady levels build with consistent dosing
Monthly LAI: Starts releasing on day 1 and can last for months after a single injection depending on product
3-month and 6-month LAIs: Designed for long coverage; missed-dose management matters because levels move slowly

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: In real clinical use, paliperidone often helps reduce psychosis symptoms and supports functioning—especially when taken consistently. Many people notice the first shifts within the first couple of weeks, but the best read on whether it’s truly working is usually closer to 4–6 weeks (and longer for some). Long-acting injections can be especially helpful when daily pill-taking is unreliable.
sections.clinical_details: Paliperidone may be used as monotherapy for schizophrenia. For schizoaffective disorder, it may be used alone or alongside mood stabilizers or antidepressants. Dose adjustments and formulation choices should be individualized based on response, tolerability, comorbidities, and patient preference—ideally with psychiatric specialist involvement.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Paliperidone is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
sections.black_box: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death. Paliperidone is not approved for the treatment of patients with dementia-related psychosis.
other: Not indicated for catatonia and may worsen psychosis and increase risk for neuroleptic malignant syndrome in patients with catatonia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): rare but life-threatening (fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability)
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) including akathisia, parkinsonism, dystonia; tardive dyskinesia risk with long-term exposure
Metabolic risks: weight gain, glucose changes, lipid changes (monitor routinely)
Hyperprolactinemia: sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, gynecomastia/galactorrhea; can affect fertility
Orthostatic hypotension/syncope and fall risk—especially with rapid titration and in older adults
QT prolongation risk—higher concern with other QT-prolonging meds or patient risk factors
Rare leukopenia/neutropenia; severe neutropenia requires discontinuation
Seizure risk: use caution in patients with lowered seizure threshold
CNS depression: can impair driving/operating machinery, especially early or with dose changes
patient_counseling: If you’re an older adult with dementia-related psychosis: this medication is not approved for that use and has a mortality warning. This is a serious conversation, not a casual one.
If you develop high fever, severe stiffness, confusion, or rapid heartbeat/sweating: treat it like an emergency (possible NMS).
If you feel intense inner restlessness (can’t sit still) or new stiffness/shaking: tell your prescriber—don’t just “push through.”
Stand up slowly. Hydrate. If you’re getting dizzy or faint, that matters—falls are not a minor side effect.
Track weight, appetite, and energy. Metabolic changes can sneak up quietly.
If sexual function, periods, breast symptoms, or lactation changes happen: say it out loud. Prolactin issues are common and treatable.
For injections: keep appointments tight. Missed-dose protocols exist for a reason—don’t improvise.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: The big buckets to know with paliperidone: movement side effects (EPS), metabolic changes (weight/glucose/lipids), prolactin-related hormone/sexual effects, dizziness/falls, sleepiness, and rare but serious reactions like NMS, severe neutropenia, and angioedema.
plain_language_list: Restlessness (akathisia) or feeling like you can’t sit still
Stiffness, tremor, slowed movement (parkinsonism), muscle tightness
Dizziness when standing (orthostatic hypotension), fainting in some cases
Weight gain and increased appetite (not always, but common enough to monitor)
Blood sugar changes and cholesterol/triglyceride changes
High prolactin: lower libido, erectile/ejaculatory issues, menstrual changes, breast tenderness/enlargement, galactorrhea
Injection site pain, swelling, redness (for LAIs)

common.incidence: Common (dose-related; varies by formulation and patient factors)
common.patient_note: EPS can look like restlessness (akathisia), stiffness/tremor/slowness (parkinsonism), or painful muscle spasms (dystonia). Tell your prescriber early—these are often fixable with dose changes, pacing titration, or targeted meds.
This is not “anxiety.” It’s a physical urge to move that can feel miserable. If it shows up during titration, that’s a red flag to reassess the plan.
Most common early and with dose changes. Higher risk in older adults and with rapid titration. Fall risk is real.
Weight gain can happen early and then continue gradually. Glucose and lipid changes can occur even if weight doesn’t move much. Monitoring isn’t optional—it’s part of safe prescribing.
This can show up as lower libido, sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, breast symptoms, or unexpected milk production. Don’t suffer in silence—there are strategies.
Some people feel sleepy or dulled, especially early. If it’s impairing your life, it’s a dosing/formulation conversation.

serious: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, severe rigidity, confusion, unstable blood pressure/heart rate. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Tardive dyskinesia: involuntary movements that can become persistent with long-term exposure; risk increases with total exposure and older age.
QT prolongation and arrhythmia risk: higher concern with other QT-prolonging meds, electrolyte issues, structural heart disease, older age, kidney impairment, or baseline QT prolongation.
Angioedema or anaphylaxis: swelling of tongue/lips/throat, trouble breathing. MEDICAL EMERGENCY.

Cerebrovascular events reported with related drugs in older adults with dementia-related psychosis; paliperidone not approved for dementia-related psychosis and carries increased mortality warning in that population.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Paliperidone has clinically important interactions even though CYP metabolism is not the main pathway. Think in terms of additive side effects (QT risk, sedation, blood pressure drops, movement side effects) and drugs that change transport/metabolism.

items.risk: Additive QTc prolongation may increase torsades de pointes risk, especially in patients with risk factors (older age, electrolyte abnormalities, structural heart disease, kidney impairment).
items.action: Avoid stacking QT-prolonging agents when possible. Consider baseline and follow-up ECGs if risk is elevated, and correct electrolytes.

items.with: Medications that lower blood pressure (antihypertensives, certain antidepressants, other antipsychotics)
items.risk: More dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, fainting, and falls.
items.action: Start low, titrate slower, counsel on standing slowly, and reassess if recurrent dizziness/falls occur.

items.with: Other CNS depressants (alcohol, sedatives, sleep meds, opioids)
items.risk: More sedation, impaired coordination, and fall risk.
items.action: Use caution, avoid unnecessary sedative stacking, and counsel on driving/operating machinery.

items.with: Dopamine agonists (used in Parkinson disease) and stimulatory dopaminergic agents
items.risk: Pharmacologic “tug-of-war” (reduced antipsychotic effect or worsened movement symptoms).
items.action: Coordinate care closely; avoid unmanaged combinations.

items.with: Carbamazepine and other strong inducers (CYP3A4/P-gp inducers)
items.risk: May lower paliperidone exposure and reduce efficacy.
items.action: Avoid if possible or monitor closely for relapse; dosing changes may be needed based on clinical response.

items.risk: Higher total dopamine blockade can increase EPS, prolactin effects, and other dose-related adverse effects (and risperidone is closely related pharmacologically).
items.action: Use specialist-guided cross-titration plans; avoid unnecessary overlap.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: With chronic psychotic disorders, switching to another treatment is usually safer than abruptly stopping. If a patient insists on stopping, gradual dose reduction over weeks to months is typically advised for oral paliperidone to reduce rebound symptoms and help detect early relapse. With long-acting injectables, a “taper” usually isn’t needed because the medication naturally leaves the body slowly—but relapse monitoring is still essential.
key_points: Oral paliperidone: If discontinuing (not switching due to urgent adverse effects), taper gradually over weeks to months when possible to reduce rebound and allow early relapse detection.
Possible withdrawal/rebound symptoms after abrupt stopping can include: agitation, anxiety, sweating, insomnia, GI symptoms, tremor, restlessness, dyskinesia, and return of psychosis symptoms.
Long-acting injectables (monthly/3-month/6-month): Withdrawal symptoms are generally less likely because elimination is slow—however, relapse can still occur and may be delayed.
If stopping is due to serious adverse effects (eg, NMS, severe neutropenia, angioedema), discontinuation and urgent medical management take priority.
Switching antipsychotics: strategies include cross-titration or abrupt switch depending on risk/urgency; high-relapse-risk patients may need overlap while the new med reaches therapeutic effect.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Paliperidone dosing depends heavily on the indication (schizophrenia vs schizoaffective vs off-label bipolar use), formulation (oral ER vs long-acting injections), kidney function, and how sensitive the patient is to side effects. Specialist-guided decisions are strongly recommended—especially for long-acting injectable conversions and missed-dose scenarios.

adult.schizophrenia_oral_initial: 6 mg PO once daily (ER tablet); for first-episode psychosis, consider 3 mg PO once daily if more sensitive to adverse effects
adult.schizophrenia_oral_titration: Increase by 3 mg/day based on response and tolerability, no sooner than every 3 days; monitor for akathisia, orthostatic hypotension, parkinsonism, and sedation during titration
adult.schizophrenia_oral_if_not_tolerated: If 6 mg/day is not tolerated, consider reducing to 3 mg/day PO
adult.schizoaffective_oral_typical: 6 mg PO once daily (ER tablet); some may do better with lower or higher doses (range 3 to 12 mg/day)
adult.schizoaffective_oral_adjustment_if_above: If exceeding 6 mg/day, increase by 3 mg/day at intervals greater than 4 days, up to 12 mg/day
adult.bipolar_mania_offlabel_oral_titration: Adjust by 3 mg increments every ≥2 days based on response and tolerability
adult.lai_sustenna_precheck: Establish tolerability with oral paliperidone, oral risperidone, or long-acting injectable risperidone prior to initiating paliperidone palmitate LAI
adult.lai_sustenna_initiation: 234 mg IM (day 1) then 156 mg IM (day 8); day 8 dose may be given between days 4 and 12 if needed
adult.lai_sustenna_oral_overlap: Oral overlap is not required after the first paliperidone palmitate injection
adult.lai_sustenna_maintenance: Begin maintenance 5 weeks after the first initiation dose: 39 to 234 mg IM every month; may administer each dose 3 to 5 weeks after the previous dose; maximum 234 mg/month
adult.lai_sustenna_missed_second_initiation_lt: Administer 156 mg ASAP, then give 117 mg 5 weeks after the first injection (regardless of timing of the 156 mg dose), then resume monthly dosing 4 weeks later
adult.lai_sustenna_missed_second_initiation_4_: Administer 156 mg ASAP, then 156 mg one week later, then resume monthly maintenance 4 weeks later
adult.lai_sustenna_missed_maintenance_4_to_6_w: Administer the missed dose ASAP, then resume usual monthly maintenance 4 weeks later
adult.lai_sustenna_missed_maintenance_gt_6_wee: Administer the usual maintenance dose ASAP, then repeat the usual maintenance dose 1 week later, then resume usual monthly dosing 4 weeks later
Administer 156 mg ASAP, then 156 mg 1 week later, then resume 234 mg monthly 4 weeks later
adult.lai_erzofri_initiation: 351 mg IM on day 1; start maintenance 4 weeks after the initial dose
adult.lai_erzofri_oral_overlap: Oral overlap is not necessary; use caution if oral paliperidone is continued after the first injection
adult.lai_erzofri_maintenance: 39 to 234 mg IM every month starting 4 weeks after the initial dose (note: 39 mg has not been studied in schizoaffective disorder); may administer each dose 3 to 5 weeks after the previous dose; maximum 234 mg/month
adult.lai_erzofri_missed_maintenance_4_to_6_we: Administer the missed dose ASAP, then resume usual monthly maintenance 4 weeks later
adult.lai_erzofri_missed_maintenance_gt_6_week: Administer the usual maintenance dose ASAP, then repeat the usual maintenance dose 1 week later, then resume usual monthly dosing 1 month later
Administer 156 mg ASAP, then 156 mg 1 week later, then resume 234 mg monthly 1 month later
adult.lai_erzofri_missed_maintenance_gt_6_mont: Administer 351 mg ASAP, then resume usual monthly maintenance 1 month later
adult.lai_trinza_requirement: Use only after at least 4 doses of monthly paliperidone LAI; the last 2 monthly doses should be the same strength before starting Trinza
adult.lai_trinza_initial: Administer when the next monthly dose is due (or 3 to 5 weeks after the last monthly dose) using the conversion based on prior monthly dose
adult.lai_trinza_maintenance: Administer the same dose every 3 months; may administer each dose 10 to 14 weeks after the previous dose; usual 273 to 819 mg every 3 months; maximum 819 mg every 3 months
adult.lai_trinza_missed_gt_3_5_months_lt_4_mon: Administer the missed dose ASAP, then resume usual 3-month dosing
adult.lai_trinza_missed_4_to_9_months: Re-load with monthly paliperidone (two injections one week apart) then resume Trinza one month later using the prior Trinza maintenance dose pathway
adult.lai_trinza_missed_gt_9_months: Reinitiate with monthly paliperidone; Trinza can be resumed after at least 4 months of adequate monthly treatment
adult.lai_hafyera_requirement: Use only after at least 4 monthly doses; the last 2 monthly doses should be the same strength before starting Hafyera (or convert from Trinza using conversion guidance)
adult.lai_hafyera_initial_from_monthly: Administer when the next monthly dose is due (or 3 to 5 weeks after the last monthly dose) using conversion guidance based on the prior monthly dose
adult.lai_hafyera_initial_from_trinza: Administer when the next 3-month dose is due (or 2.5 to 3.5 months after the last Trinza dose) using conversion guidance based on prior Trinza dose
adult.lai_hafyera_maintenance: Administer the same dose every 6 months; may administer each dose 22 to 27 weeks after the previous dose; usual 1,092 to 1,560 mg every 6 months; maximum 1,560 mg every 6 months
adult.lai_hafyera_missed_gt_6_months_3_weeks_l: Do not give the missed Hafyera dose. Give 156 mg monthly paliperidone ASAP, then 1,092 mg Hafyera one month later, then resume every 6 months
Do not give the missed Hafyera dose. Give 234 mg monthly paliperidone ASAP, then 1,560 mg Hafyera one month later, then resume every 6 months
adult.lai_hafyera_missed_8_to_11_months_1092: Do not give the missed Hafyera dose. Give 156 mg monthly paliperidone on day 1 and day 8, then 1,092 mg Hafyera one month after day 8, then resume every 6 months
adult.lai_hafyera_missed_8_to_11_months_1560: Do not give the missed Hafyera dose. Give 156 mg monthly paliperidone on day 1 and day 8, then 1,560 mg Hafyera one month after day 8, then resume every 6 months
adult.lai_hafyera_missed_gt_11_months: Reinitiate with monthly paliperidone; Hafyera can be resumed after at least 4 months of adequate monthly treatment
adult.renal_adjustment_oral_crcl_50_to_79: Initial 3 mg PO once daily; maximum 6 mg PO once daily
adult.renal_adjustment_oral_crcl_10_to_49: Initial 1.5 mg PO once daily (or 3 mg every other day); maximum 3 mg PO once daily
adult.renal_adjustment_lai_general: Avoid long-acting injectable paliperidone when kidney function is changing, because dosing is hard to safely adjust; consider an alternative antipsychotic
adult.renal_adjustment_sustenna_crcl_50_to_79_: 156 mg IM day 1, then 117 mg IM 1 week later
78 mg IM monthly starting 5 weeks after the first initiation dose; may adjust to 39 to 156 mg monthly; maximum 156 mg/month
adult.renal_adjustment_erzofri_crcl_50_to_79_m: 78 mg IM monthly starting 1 month after the initial dose; may adjust to 39 to 156 mg monthly; maximum 156 mg/month
adult.renal_adjustment_lai_crcl_10_to_49: Use of long-acting injectable formulations is not recommended
adult.renal_adjustment_dialysis: Avoid use (not significantly dialyzable; risk outweighs benefit in hemodialysis/peritoneal dialysis/CRRT/PIRRT settings)
adult.hepatic_adjustment_mild_to_moderate: No dosage adjustment necessary (Child-Pugh A or B)
adult.hepatic_adjustment_severe: Not well studied; use caution and specialist guidance
adult.older_adult_guidance: Avoid for behavioral problems in dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic options failed and there is risk of harm; for labeled indications (eg, schizophrenia), use lower-end dosing, titrate slowly, and monitor closely

sections.simple_explanation: Oral Invega is a once-daily extended-release tablet. The injection versions (paliperidone palmitate) are designed for monthly, every-3-month, or every-6-month dosing. The upside of injections is adherence and stability. The downside is that dose changes and side effects can take longer to fully show up—and missed-dose protocols are more complicated.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Paliperidone requires extra planning in pregnancy, postpartum, older adulthood, and kidney impairment. The goal is shared decision-making: protect psychiatric stability while minimizing avoidable risk.
sections.pregnancy: Paliperidone crosses the placenta. As a class, second-generation antipsychotics have not shown a large signal for major congenital malformations, but data specific to paliperidone are limited. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics can cause newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, abnormal tone, feeding issues, respiratory distress, somnolence, tremor). Tapering late in pregnancy to reduce newborn symptoms is not recommended. If treatment is needed, use the lowest effective dose of a single agent and monitor metabolic risk during pregnancy.
sections.lactation: Paliperidone can be present in breast milk (and is the active metabolite of risperidone). If breastfeeding during treatment, monitor the infant for excess sedation, poor feeding, failure to thrive, jitteriness, and abnormal movements. Extra caution is warranted in premature or low-birth-weight infants and if other sedating meds are used.
sections.pediatrics: Paliperidone is used in adolescents for schizophrenia (age thresholds depend on labeling and local practice). Pediatric patients have higher vulnerability to metabolic changes (weight gain, glucose and lipid effects), movement side effects, and prolactin effects. Avoid rapid discontinuation due to risk of withdrawal and emergent dystonia/dyskinesia; taper gradually when stopping unless urgent safety issues require abrupt change.
sections.geriatrics: Beers Criteria flags antipsychotics as higher-risk in adults ≥65, especially for dementia-related behavioral symptoms due to increased stroke risk, cognitive decline, and mortality. Avoid for dementia-related behaviors unless nonpharmacologic approaches failed and there is risk of harm. If used for appropriate indications like schizophrenia, use lower doses, titrate slowly, and monitor closely for orthostasis, falls, EPS, sedation, and sodium abnormalities (SIADH/hyponatremia risk).
sections.hepatic: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment: no adjustment generally needed. Severe hepatic impairment: not well studied—use caution and specialist guidance.
sections.renal: Kidney function matters a lot for paliperidone. Dose reductions are recommended for oral ER in reduced CrCl. Long-acting injectables may be inappropriate in moderate-to-severe impairment and should be avoided when kidney function is changing because the dose cannot be safely fine-tuned quickly.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mental status and functioning at every visit: psychosis intensity, mood symptoms, sleep, agitation, insight, and day-to-day functioning
Adherence at every visit (especially if on oral): missed doses can look like “med stopped working” when it’s really inconsistent exposure
EPS checks at every visit; use a formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if higher risk): akathisia, parkinsonism, dystonia, dyskinesia/tardive dyskinesia
Fall risk at every visit: orthostatic symptoms, gait stability, sedation, and recent falls
Vital signs at every visit: BP (including orthostatics when relevant), pulse, temperature; increased frequency early in treatment and after dose changes
Weight/BMI: check around 8 and 12 weeks after starting or changing dose, then at least quarterly (many clinicians check at every visit)
Glucose monitoring (fasting glucose or HbA1c): around 4 months after initiation, then at least annually (more often if abnormal)
Lipid panel: around 4 months after initiation, then at least annually (more often if abnormal)
Metabolic risk history annually: personal/family history of obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, cardiovascular disease
Prolactin: ask about symptoms at every visit until dose is stable; check a level if symptoms appear (menstrual changes, sexual dysfunction, gynecomastia, galactorrhea)
CBC as clinically indicated; monitor more frequently early if history of low WBC or drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia
Kidney function and electrolytes periodically (and more often if risk factors exist), because renal clearance and QT risk factors matter
ECG when clinically indicated (QT risk factors, symptoms, or QT-prolonging combinations)
Injection site reactions and schedule integrity for LAIs: track last injection date, product, dose, and plan for missed-dose protocols

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Paliperidone comes as a once-daily ER tablet and multiple long-acting injectable options. The formulation choice is often about adherence, relapse risk, and how comfortable a patient is with injections versus daily pills.
items: Oral extended-release tablet (Invega / paliperidone ER): 3 mg, 6 mg, 9 mg (some markets also have 1.5 mg)
Monthly IM paliperidone palmitate: Invega Sustenna (39 mg, 78 mg, 117 mg, 156 mg, 234 mg) and Erzofri (39 mg, 78 mg, 117 mg, 156 mg, 234 mg, 351 mg)
3-month IM paliperidone palmitate: Invega Trinza (273 mg, 410 mg, 546 mg, 819 mg)
6-month IM paliperidone palmitate: Invega Hafyera (1,092 mg, 1,560 mg)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Paliperidone is the primary active metabolite of risperidone. In plain English: it reduces overactive dopamine signaling (D2 blockade) and also blocks certain serotonin receptors (especially 5-HT2A). That dopamine-serotonin combo is a big part of how atypical antipsychotics can reduce hallucinations and delusions while sometimes being better tolerated than older antipsychotics—though paliperidone still has a meaningful movement side effect risk, especially as dose increases.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Paliperidone is a core option for schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder, especially when the goals include symptom control plus relapse prevention. The long-acting injectable forms are often used when adherence is inconsistent, when relapse risk is high, or when a patient prefers the simplicity of injections. The tradeoff is that LAIs are slower to adjust—so you want a careful plan, good monitoring, and a prescriber who knows the conversion and missed-dose rules cold. It is not approved for dementia-related psychosis and carries an increased mortality warning in that population.

seo.title: Paliperidone (Invega): Uses, Dosing (Oral & Injections), Side Effects & Monitoring
seo.description: Paliperidone (Invega) for schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder: oral ER vs long-acting injections (Sustenna, Trinza, Hafyera), dosing basics, missed-dose rules, side effects (EPS, weight/metabolic, prolactin), and key safety warnings.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Paliperidone is used to treat schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. It can reduce hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, disorganized thinking, and mood symptoms tied to psychosis.

faqs.q: How long does Invega take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice early changes within 1 to 2 weeks, but the more reliable improvements often build over 4 to 6 weeks. The timeline depends on the symptom profile, dose, and how consistent dosing is.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between Invega and Invega Sustenna/Trinza/Hafyera?
faqs.a: Invega is a once-daily extended-release tablet. Invega Sustenna is a monthly injection, Trinza is every 3 months, and Hafyera is every 6 months. The injection forms are designed to improve adherence and reduce relapse risk tied to missed pills, but dose changes and side effects can take longer to fully show up.

It can. Paliperidone is associated with weight gain and metabolic changes (blood sugar and cholesterol/triglycerides). That’s why weight, HbA1c/glucose, and lipids are monitored routinely—especially after starting or changing the dose.

faqs.q: Can paliperidone cause movement side effects?
faqs.a: Yes. Paliperidone can cause EPS (extrapyramidal symptoms) مثل akathisia (inner restlessness), parkinsonism (stiffness/tremor/slowness), and dystonia (muscle spasms). Tell your prescriber early—these can often be improved by adjusting dose, slowing titration, or adding targeted treatments.

faqs.q: Why does paliperidone affect prolactin and sex hormones?
faqs.a: By blocking dopamine (especially in pathways that regulate prolactin), paliperidone can raise prolactin levels. That can lead to sexual dysfunction, low libido, erectile/ejaculatory issues, menstrual changes, breast tenderness/enlargement, or galactorrhea. If symptoms show up, clinicians can check prolactin and discuss options.

faqs.q: Is paliperidone safe in older adults with dementia-related psychosis?
faqs.a: This is a major red flag area. Antipsychotics carry an increased risk of death in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis, and paliperidone is not approved for dementia-related psychosis. If this situation comes up, it should be a serious risk-benefit discussion with a clinician.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off paliperidone?
faqs.a: If you’re stopping oral paliperidone (and it’s not an emergency situation), gradual dose reduction over weeks to months is usually recommended to reduce rebound symptoms and catch early relapse. With long-acting injections, a formal taper usually isn’t needed because levels fall slowly—but relapse monitoring is still essential.

faqs.q: What if I miss my Invega Sustenna injection?
faqs.a: There are specific missed-dose protocols based on how long it’s been since the last injection (and whether you’re still in the initiation phase or maintenance). Don’t guess—call your clinic. Timing matters because the re-loading strategy can change depending on whether it’s been weeks versus months.

faqs.q: Does kidney function matter with paliperidone?
faqs.a: Yes—big time. Paliperidone is cleared largely through the kidneys. Oral ER dosing is reduced with lower creatinine clearance, and long-acting injectables may be inappropriate in moderate-to-severe impairment or when kidney function is changing because you can’t easily fine-tune a depot dose.
